utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution motion for the protection of witnesses and victims. Ms. Hollis, so we can discuss the programme, as it were, we will sit this afternoon until sometime just before four o'clock, and if we have not completed matters, we will go on tomorrow morning. There is one of your motions which must be discussed in closed session in any event, and we can deal with that at the same time as we deal with the status conference which will follow the hearing of the motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there is anything anybody wants to say about the order, I propose we start with the motion to protect the victims and witnesses, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. For the purposes of this motion and other motions, we will be arguing this afternoon, the Prosecution relies in major part on the pleadings already filed, and based upon that will endeavour to make our oral remarks succinct and hopefully very much to the point. In regard to the general motion we have filed for protection for victims and witnesses, we would like to make the following points, Your Honours: First of all, that the request is consistent with the mandate that is set forth in Article 22 and is well within the Rules of the Tribunal. Also, the requested relief is based on justifiable concerns about the security and privacy of witnesses who will come before this Tribunal. The requested relief also affords the accused an adequate opportunity to prepare to meet the charge against him or to prepare a defence if he chooses to present a defence. While giving the accused the means to adequately prepare the request -- to adequately prepare for this trial, the requested relief does reinforce that material that is provided to the Defence through discovery is for use in preparing for this trial and for no other use and protects witnesses and victims from disclosure for unrelated uses. It appropriately precludes disclosure to the public at large or, for that matter, to other Defence attorneys or accused in other cases unless a showing can be made that it is relevant and appropriate. It also appropriately precludes disclosure of discovery material to the media which may have been done in this case. Such disclosure is inappropriate and should not be allowed. The Prosecution, with this requested relief, has attempted to fashion a relief that would allow appropriate use of discovery material by the Defence, but at the same time would protect victims and witnesses from inappropriate use of that material. We ask you to grant the motion. It is reasonable. It is based upon a sufficient basis, and it is well within your discretion and the mandate of the statute to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It has been the practice in other cases, of course, to make similar orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so that I can follow what it is you are asking for, Ms. Hollis, is an order to the Defence not to disclose the names or whereabouts of victims and witnesses, not to disclose the witness statements or the contents of other documents which may identify a victim or witness, except as necessary for the preparation of the defence. That is, in general terms, what is asked for, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And your reasons for doing so is that there have been cases in which there have been breaches of confidentiality and security, and you have concerns about this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. In addition to that, of course, there are continuing tensions, there continues to be the fact that other persons who have been indicted have not yet been apprehended, there are other suspects who have not yet been indicted, so that the opportunities exist outside this Tribunal, in all the areas in which witnesses and victims are located, the potential exists for physical threats to these witnesses, for harassment, and for intimidation. So that it is not just based upon prior incidents that have occurred but the continuing situation regarding these victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You refer to disclosure to the media. I mean, is there anything in particular you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have put a concern in our -- one of our pleadings before this chamber concerning an Article that was written, and in the Article there is specific reference made to material that was provided to the Defence by the Prosecution as part of the discovery material that simply reinforces our concern that without a protective order, material will be provided to the media without first showing the Trial Chamber the necessity for that type of wide distribution of sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, in effect, the order would preclude the Defence from disclosing any document unless it could be shown that it was necessary for the defence or the preparation of the defence, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Certainly to the media, Your Honour, they would have to make such a showing, in terms of preparation of their case, they would have to decide what the limited circumstances are that would require the type of disclosure this relief allows for. That would be based upon their professional judgement within the parameters of the relief requested. We do not ask that they must come to this Trial Chamber every time they wish to disclose the name of a witness or to disclose information from a statement if that disclosure is based upon their professional judgement that it is necessary in this limited circumstance to provide that information to adequately prepare their defence. But that goes for members of the public, not for the public at large, nor for the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the Defence response, there is a suggestion that they should be allowed to interview the Prosecution witnesses before they are called to testify. You have dealt with that in your reply, suggesting you oppose that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Only to those witnesses who do not consent to such interviews, Your Honour, and we have undertaken to contact the witnesses in our case to ask them if they are agreeable to a pre-trial interview with the Defence here in The Hague, and we will pass that information on to the Defence. To the extent these witnesses are agreeable, of course, we have absolutely no concern about that happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the normal practice here?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That has been in the past, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the practice in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In terms of most of the civilian jurisdictions in terms of criminal case, it is my understanding that that is the practice that they cannot be forced to conduct interviews or to accede to interviews, although that may then be raised as a means of delay after cross-examination. I come from the military system, and in the military, if we are dealing with a military witness, they can be ordered to speak to the defence, but if we're dealing with a civilian witness, they can't be ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the system to which I am accustomed, there is no question of the Defence interviewing Prosecution witnesses before the trial unless there are some very unusual circumstances. The practice is not to allow that to happen for the sort of reasons which you mention in your pleadings. Judge Mumba comes from a similar background. However, you are prepared to ask the witnesses whether they are prepared to be interviewed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have begun that process, in fact, of calling them and asking them, and we will provide the information to the Defence as we obtain it from the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter which has been raised is a request as to whether the witnesses have been interviewed by security or intelligence services or other organisations that have interviewed them for counselling purposes. Again, can you assist on that, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In regard to the request for disclosure of whether witnesses have received psychiatric or psychological treatment, again we have undertaken to ask our witnesses if, in fact, they have received such treatment and to convey that information to the Defence. The Defence also attaches to that particular request that all the records of any such treatment or counselling that has occurred be obtained by the Prosecution and provided to the Trial Chamber. That portion of their request we object to. We believe that, first of all, the request itself is based upon speculation as to what are termed "activist psychiatrist" in the United States and other speculative grounds, but as to records, we believe that without a showing of the relevance and a narrowing or a definition of what they mean by “activist psychiatrist" and who they may have in mind, that that is an overly broad request that would at this point unduly invade the privacy of these witnesses and so we do object to the portion concerning records. We also question our authority to go to many of these countries and to order psychiatrists in those countries to produce records that may be protected under various laws in various countries. So that portion of their request, we do object to. And, Your Honour, in terms of their request that they be told of any type of interrogation, counselling, or the rendering of any type of assistance to these witnesses from state security and intelligence services or social or religious organisations, we object to this request on the grounds that this request is overly broad and it is unsupported by justifying why such a labour-intensive request should be embarked upon at this point. For example, how do they define "state security and intelligence services"? What services would they include within that? How do they define "social and religious organisations"? What organisations would they include within that? Without defining these, without showing the relevance and explaining why this cannot be brought out on cross-examination, we suggest that the requested relief is unwarranted at this time and that it is not shown to be relevant, it is too broad, and that at this point in time, it is an unwarranted intrusion into the lives and circumstances of these witnesses. As we pointed out in our pleading in response to this requested relief, we have witnesses coming before this Tribunal who basically have been left without the means to exist. They're outside their homelands, many of them, or they have returned to a different area than the one they lived in. Many of them for years were denied the ability to actually earn their livelihood because they were in other countries that would not allow them to pursue their professions. Many of them were traumatised. Of course, they received relief from many, many agencies. That is not a sufficient basis to require this kind of disclosure to the Defence. We would suggest and we would ask that without a further showing of relevance and why it cannot be adequately addressed on cross-examination, that this Defence request be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so if you would remind me, please, what you are prepared to ask the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honour, we are not prepared to ask them anything. We believe the list of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you said earlier you were prepared to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, two things: Number 1, are they willing to engage in pre-trial interviews here in the Hague with Defence counsel, and in that regard, Your Honour, we do point out Defence counsel, because were the accused to be present at such an interview, the request may be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be wholly wrong if any such suggestion were made, but I don't think that is a suggestion which is made.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So we will ask them if they are willing to speak with Defence counsel here in the Hague, we will convey that to the Defence, those witnesses who are willing to do so, we can make adequate arrangements when they arrive here in the Hague. Secondly, we will inquire of our witnesses if they have received psychiatric or psychological counselling or treatment, and we will convey that information to the Defence. If you have no further questions, Your Honours, I have no further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, it may be convenient to deal with these matters, but technically, of course, I suppose there should be a motion in respect of them. But it may be convenient to deal with them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honour, for convenience and expediency, we did treat what was contained in their response as a separate motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Who is going to deal with this for the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I do have a great deal of understanding and feeling for suffering that the victims and the witnesses have gone through, on one hand. On the other hand, it is my duty to make sure that only credible evidence is presented before you, that cross-examination process be such that it ferrets out all the biases that could have consciously or unconsciously influenced the perception and recollection of those witnesses, and if you are going to have, and indeed, a fair hearing and to have a crystal clear evidence before you, the Defence ought to be given a certain latitude to interview the witnesses just as Your Honour presented, and here is not only a difficulty that might be facing the witnesses that are coming from Bosnia but at the same time there is the same amount of difficulties that are being encountered by counsel, both of us coming from the United States, going into the areas that we are strangers by the most recently political divisions of this war, that we will be facing physical risks to ourselves, at the same time attempting to even contact these witnesses there would present first difficulties to the witnesses, if we were to follow traditional practices as Your Honour suggested that would be usually followed in the national jurisdiction where the investigators of the Defence team would contact the witnesses and ask whether or not they wish or not to communicate to the Defence team. We don't have that luxury. That privilege might be theoretical, but it's not real. And in our response to the Prosecutor's motion, I apologise to Your Honours, but we were on the eve of the trial and, you know, I know it would have been a bit more proper to address the formal motion, but within the context of this motion, I was asking just for a broader latitude that we would get a chance to investigate the background of the witnesses and -- but not only the background because the statements that we have received so far, even on these 25 statements that we got a few weeks ago, we have gotten those statements from Tadic's trial and Tadic's trial was not a genocide, and all the relevant testimony referred to unrelated counts to the count which is not related to my client Dr. Kovacevic, if we don't have a chance to talk to almost all these witnesses now, these statements might be wholly irrelevant. They are talking about, you know, another man sitting in one detention centre or camps as it may be, but the area about the plan, implementation, alleged participation of Dr. Kovacevic, his personal intent or his ability or inability to stop what has been allegedly happening, it's none of those statements. So that means we are going into this trial without having any information of what those witnesses are going to say. I know the Office of the Prosecutor is overwhelmed with work, I know that judicial economy in this Chamber -- this Chamber's high views of the Defendant's right to speedy trial have been prevailing on all of us, but, however, in order to have a fair trial, we ought to be given a chance to examine the aspects or the witnesses' statements that haven't been heretofore presented to us in order to go along with this Trial Chamber, I for reason of expediency and practicality suggested that we, as Defence, be given a chance to interview the Prosecutor's witnesses here in The Hague. First, for protection of the witnesses. The community in which they live will not be alarmed by strangers coming to talk to them. They will be here because, knowing that they are here to testify, whether they will have an hour or two conference with the Defence attorney in the presence of the investigator or a Prosecutor, that would be just fine with us. And I have suggested, in order to facilitate the same thing, we would allow the Defence witnesses, just when we begin our case in chief, if we go that far, to give the same courtesy to the Prosecution. Another point: We -- what happened to us most recently, after we had a conference before Your Honours on 27th of March, none of those wishes have materialised. We really haven't had the benefit of any of those suggestions that Your Honour requested that be given to us in our investigation. Moreover, we were surprised. I asked could I be escorted to go to a Moslem theatre of international police, they said we don't know anything about it, we don't have staff. Why don't you go over there and talk to the commander of the police on the other side and he's going to talk to the local police and the local policeman is going to bring the witness where? In the police station for questioning? I was shocked when I walked in <unintelligble> because the Serbs were rounded up and were questioned in the police station because there was another order came, not from this chamber but from another chamber of this court. I don't think that -- those are not the intents and wishes of this court. But when the clear water starts from here and goes downstream, there are a lot of people that don't have an understanding of the law and the intents and wishes of this court and muddy it up. That's why I figured if this process is going, should be as pristine as it is, we could cooperate professionally and give this courtesy to each other here. Let it come similar to interviewing the witnesses. Another point is on -- let me start first about state agencies. I understand these are people who are displaced and dispossessed, and if we have this as a form of a questionnaire where they would state: "I have received aid from such and such social organisation. For that matter I know personally because I have maybe 10 percent of my practice in Chicago are a member of the Moslem community from Bosnia who ask for my services. I know the various social organisations they are receiving help. I know of a psychiatrist with University of Illinois that's counselling and interviewing quite a few witnesses. There was a story in a Chicago paper and he's using the method where he is hypnotising the witnesses, getting information to them, and after he's waking them up, he is talking to them about it. I'm not quite sure of the tale but that is an account of the story. After I talked to psychiatrist, he said, recollection of the evidence or the memory is suppressed. That is kind of modern school of thought. The opponents of that school of thought practically call it an "implant memory" where in psychiatrists who believe what the reality should be, talking to the patients later on what the defence should be. If the psychiatrist knows that these people are -- talking about people from Kozarac that have been attending these courts, and if this has been happening, you ought to know. We ought to know. We don't want to harm their treatment. But we want to find out, is this charlatanism or are you going to get somebody's witnesses through hypnosis or are you going to get the testimony from these witnesses as to what indeed happened. That is on this particular point, and it's very important because I think that -- in a very scientific, professional journals this type of approach has been discredited, and for that reason we want to present all that evidence before you, whether it is possible or not. For a Prosecutor to come the day before such a witness is to testify that he had treatment through such a clinic would be to derail the efficiency of this trial. We ought to know about it. We have to have to get our expert, we have to review -- have expert review that evidence. We need time to do it. What I'm suggesting, I am merely identifying the problems so that everybody should, in a professional manner, be informed about it. If the witnesses have had psychiatric treatment and somebody has heard some serious problem about perceiving reality, conditions as paranoia, schizophrenia or something like that, this is indeed highly relevant whether they are capable to perceive the events as they are or not, they are capable to recall them. That's why those major things are so important. If somebody had marital stress problems, we certainly wouldn't be interested in that. Financial rewards have been always at issue in examining the witness. It is not whether somebody has received money, but if somebody received something other of value in order to perpetuate certain kind of testimony. We are not asking that any monetary amounts be disclosed if subsistence has been provided by the various social or religious organisation, but if these amounts have been a little more than usual social agencies in any of the western countries provide, these become relevant. We have to look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you any reason for making that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The most recent one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What happened in Tadic's case, there was a witness, L. I think that was a fabricated testimony that came up before the Trial Chamber at that time. And I apologise to everybody because I don't know the -- indeed all the facts about it. I wasn't at that case. But the general impression that the people I talked to, it was somehow swept under the rug. We want this trial to be impeccable. We will give all those information you are requesting of the Prosecution on any witness that we are presenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: During the trial -- during the trial, Mr. Vucicevic, you can ask the witnesses these questions, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we could. But at that time it is going to be highly ineffective, because if the correct answer doesn't come out of the witness, we will never have a chance to check it, verify it, and disprove it. It's kind of closing the door of the barn when the horse is out. Let's check the barn to see whether the horse is there or not early on. I am not a Doubting Thomas, but it seems in this type of practice we prevent contamination of those or indeed real impossible things. As I said, minor things about, you know, minor psychiatric counselling, stress at work, immediate stress after displacement, I understand. But prolonged psychiatric testimony, payment of -- or position of, you know, political, governmental that were given to certain witnesses, we ought to know. To these witnesses to us are going to be names that we are going to see even if we are allowed. What I see with this method, it is highly unreliable. We are entitled to ask at trial the witness, if he says, did you refuse to talk to us or not and he says, "Well, I don't remember." He might not remember a call from the Prosecutor. That remember is nothing. But if he was going to say or he or she, truth, nothing but the truth, he had no reason not to talk to us, and if he had a reason, you ought to hear those reasons. With a simple question from them that is going to be lost. What I'm suggesting, the witness could -- we could design a little questionnaire, they could pass it to the witness, witness could fill it out, we will have a record before you. I mean, you know, I'm afraid that this is going to be, to a great degree, a trial by surprise because we have Tadic's testimony, we don't know anything about witnesses, we can't learn about, you know, their psychological problems, we can't learn anything about whether there was a financial benefits in their lives, and we don't know whether there has been any coaching, counselling, or preparation for, God forbid, fabricated testimony, but there are so many governments there that are interested in the outcomes of these trials, and I think that we all have to be, you know, mindful of that. That was the reason for my -- I was not getting prepared, nor ever entertained a thought that it should be a fishing expedition, just a bare necessity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, we are minded to rule on this matter tomorrow morning. Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe we have sufficiently covered the points we wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I should mention that there has been a ruling of this Tribunal, one of the Trial Chambers, in Delalic in March of last year, and during the course of a ruling, the Trial Chamber there rejected the submission of the Defence that it had a right to the addresses of the witnesses for the purposes of conducting pre-trial interviews, and there was a ruling, as I say, of a Trial Chamber, but we will, of course, have to consider this matter afresh. Very well. That leads us to the next motion, which is the motion in relation to the investigator. This is a motion to allow the investigator in charge of the matter to observe the proceedings and not to be precluded from being called as a witness. The rules allow for that. Is there anything you particularly want to add to what you have already submitted on paper, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, we suggest that regarding the Defence response, that the rule applies to both parties to the trial, so there is no inappropriate advantage to one party or the other. Also, that the Defence interpretation of the Rule and the restrictions the Defence would ask you to place on the Rule simply are not supported by the plain language of the Rule itself, nor by any reasonable inferences you can draw from that plain language. We certainly agree that this is not an absolute and that there may be contexts in which a lead investigator could not hear evidence and then testify, such as if the lead investigator himself or herself were a victim or a witness to events that were relevant to an indictment. Such is not the case here, nor has such a case been put forward by the Defence. The Prosecution is concerned with two implications of the Defence argument and would specifically wish to address the Trial Chamber regarding those. The first is this: To the extent the Defence argues that the lead investigator in this case would commit perjury before this Trial Chamber or any judicial body we strenuously object to such an unfounded accusation. Secondly, to the extent the Defence argument on this matter suggests that the Prosecution in this case would suborn perjury or would allow such to occur with our knowledge, the Prosecution again strenuously objects to such unfounded accusations. Again, Your Honour, we believe the motion basically speaks for itself and is consistent with the plain language of Rule 90E. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Prosecution feel offended by their reading of my response, I would apologise to them. However, the response has not been written with the words they use, merely the noted hypothetical, and it did not imply at all that they would ever use it. However, since we are anticipating the future, my reading of the Rule 90D contains two clauses, and the Prosecutor was trying to more or less disembowel the rule by using exception to make the main reading of the Rule. Sub-rule D says, "A witness other than an expert who has not testified shall not be present when the testimony of another witness is given." That's a basic rule. And the Prosecutor might be allowed to testify later; I believe that there was some special, extraordinary circumstance, either he should have been there following the trial. To me, investigator is just close to the case, to the theory of a case, everything, just as an attorney. And in most rules of professional conduct, and even the rules of professional conduct that the defence attorneys are bound before this Court, indicates that lawyers shall not be testifying. To me it seems that this invitation is here being asked of you. I tried to strain and find a reason why it could be, and, you know, I suggested indeed for exceptional circumstances would have been exceptionally stringent test, and that I submitted to you a three-prong test where investigator could be testifying, and that could be if a fact has been discovered after the trial has started, or just shortly before the trial, if you may wish to expand, that that fact was unduly hidden from the Prosecutor and that such a fact cannot be proven by any other witness. But to allow what is an exception to kind of disembowel the Rule, I don't need that kind of attitude, it fosters opportunistic behaviour. In anybody, whether men, attorneys, and that could happen. And if the Rule is going to have its import as it intended, as I see that intent, this exception should be read as an exception. I did not suggest that this team of Prosecutors, whom I have gotten experience to respect and work with, would ever do it. But, as they say, circumstances change, because they have said -- that's their language -- they do not intend to call Miss Inayat in, but if the circumstances change, and that's what we're talking. We're talking about something that the Rule says it shouldn't happen; however, we should narrow it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you wish your investigator, in due course, to be present or not, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would only wish my investigator to testify under the same stringent circumstances as I have suggested. If my investigator is in the court listening to any other witness testifying, I wouldn't want him to come back and testify on the same matter. I wouldn't feel very proud of myself doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall grant this motion. Rule 90(E) is quite clear. It permits an investigator to be called as a witness notwithstanding that the investigator has been present in the courtroom. We can see no reason in this case not to allow that Rule to operate, no reason has been put forward before us why it should not, and therefore, as has been the practice in the Tribunal, at least as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned, the investigator may be present. The motion is granted. We will turn to the next matter which I mentioned, and that is the Defence motion calling for a Prosecutor's code of conduct, opposed by the Prosecutor, and we will hear the Defence upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, the Defence is bound by a code of professional conduct for all proceedings in this Tribunal, and the Prosecutor is not bound by such a code. If I may have a moment to talk a tiny bit about political theory? The two kinds of government that we know in this world, one is the political realm and one is the judicial realm. Montequeu <check name> and many others pointed out the fundamental difference. In the political world, one might say the ends justify the means. Political people are trying to achieve the right ends for society, and sometimes it means proceeding in ways that might violate certain moral codes, codes of honesty, even legal codes to achieve these ends. We're all very familiar with politics. On the other hand, the judicial form of rule in the world says that the means are tremendously important, that the means cannot be slighted in any way, even though it costs money, even though it takes time, even though it requires a great deal of what the politicians might call "inefficiency." A trial is premised on the notion that we're not sure what justice is if we don't have fair means of proving justice. It's not clear to us whether the ends are right or wrong unless we have fair procedures. I think a statement was made that students will read for hundreds of years in the Tadic trial that the very legality of this Tribunal is a function of its fairness, that one may doubt whether the Security Council, under Chapters 6 and 7, had the authority, one may question that back and forth, but over the long run, it's the fairness of the procedures that count. In that respect, it seems to me that a Court of Justice must have a level playing field and must require that both sides adhere to the standards of professional conduct and honesty so that the means are never subordinated to any ends. The Prosecutor has responded to our substitute motion, and let me quote the operative language of the Prosecutor's response in saying "that it is the 'Tribunal' which prosecutes persons, not the Office of the Prosecutor, the substitute motion is, in effect, requesting this Trial Chamber to include all members of the Tribunal as 'prosecutors' who would be bound by this proposed code of conduct. So, trial and appellate judges, all members of the Chambers' support staff and all members of the Registry would be subject to a code of conduct promulgated by the Prosecutor." Since this is the operative statement of their response, let me simply point out that the relief that we request, respectfully request, the Trial Chamber to rule that appearances and practices before this tribunal by attorneys from the Office of the Prosecutor shall be barred unless the Prosecutor submits a professional code of conduct. So the horrible situation that they envisage has nothing at all to do with the relief we ask. We have asked to make it a condition precedent that attorneys from the Prosecutor's Office must come into this Tribunal bound by a professional code of prosecutorial conduct because that is integral to what they stand for. If the Prosecution sees in an indictment procedure, for example, where there is no one else present, it's just the Prosecutor and the reviewing judge -- so it's an ex parte proceeding, it's very important, it's the first thing that happens in a case -- the reviewing Judge is entitled to know that the Prosecution is coming before the reviewing Judge bound by a code of conduct, that this is not a political situation, that this is not something that flows from politics but this is something that is going to a Tribunal. To be confident that the Prosecutor is bound by that code, one can say that the Prosecutor must subscribe to that code before appearing before the reviewing Judge. Now, it seems to me this Tribunal has all the power it needs to impose a condition like that because, as I say, it's integrally related to the very reviewing of the indictment procedure. And if that's true at that end, it's true all the way down, that in every step of the way, when the Prosecutor comes here, it's with that idea that it is bound by a code of professional conduct. The Prosecutor says the substitute motion is based on no alleged misconduct of the Prosecution in this case and therefore it's frivolous. Well, the Defence attorneys are bound by a defence code and you haven't shown us that we have engaged in any misconduct, and I don't think that's an appropriate matter. I am perfectly happy to be bound by a Defence code of professional conduct, whether or not the thought would ever occur to me to engage in any unprofessional conduct, and I certainly would never entertain that. So it's not a question of "Let's wait and see until there is misconduct before we then impose a code." We do that in advance. It's a prophylactic Rule rather than a Rule that is one that is set up only if something like that happens. We might never know that there is misconduct. One of the ideas of a code is to hold people to a sense of ethics that might weed out potential abuses before they ever occur because it's not always clear when misconduct occurs. Sometimes it's not detectable. And one last word. This Tribunal might deny this motion, but I think, if you want to do so, Your Honours, I don't think this is going to go away. I think the next case will bring it up and the case after that and the media, and the more important the cases are, the more Defence counsel will continue to say, "Why should we be bound by rules when they're not?" I think it's a matter of fundamental fairness, and I submit that this is the time to face up to it and to impose such a requirement on the Prosecution rather than have it come up again and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, you said, perhaps by a slip of the tongue, "this Tribunal might deny this motion." But that's an important point, isn't it? You are asking the Trial Chamber to make an order of this sort affecting the whole Prosecution and the whole Tribunal, not simply this trial. So the question must be: Even if we were minded to grant the motion, would we have any power to impose such a code on the Prosecutor or, indeed, anybody else? How are we to make such an order in a trial of this sort? It's a matter for the Tribunal as a whole, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: That's a good question, Your Honour. I think that our very limited jurisdiction as Defence counsel is to say we are entitled to fairness in our trial and we are entitled for them to come into a code as to this trial. Whether the Prosecution takes that as a good hint that the same code perhaps should be effectuated to guide itself in all cases, it would be up to them. But I think that if we were to win this motion limited to this particular trial at this particular time, other defendants and other people will probably say, "Well, we want the benefit of that too." I can't go to a different Chamber -- I mean, you have jurisdiction over me now, and I think this is the appropriate place for me to raise the motion because it impacts on what we're going to be doing when the trial starts, so I think it's appropriate and correct and jurisdictionally correct for me to bring up the motion with respect to this trial. But if it is extended, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, Your Honour, we suggest to you that there is a fundamental difference between persons who appear here on behalf of the Prosecutor and Defence counsel who appear here on behalf of various accused. When the Tribunal was set up, there was created an Office of the Prosecutor, and I do not appear here on behalf of Brenda Hollis, I appear here on behalf of the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor is a person who is appointed and has certain responsibilities as an appointed official under the United Nations, also has responsibilities that are set forth in the statute that govern the types of conduct she must carry out herself and must ensure that her staff carries out. So in the creation of the Tribunal, we have created a sub-organ with a person at its head who is fully accountable to the Tribunal and to the United Nations for breaches of conduct the United Nations expects and breaches of conduct that are set forth in various articles of the statute and in the rules. Let's contrast that to the Defence counsel who come in here as independent contractors. There is no Office of the Defence for the Tribunal, so there is no defender or Defence counsel who is in a similar situation as the Prosecutor. So there is no one who has responsibility by virtue of their position as the head of a UN organ within a UN organisation to be accountable for conduct under the statute and under the rules. That's a fundamental difference. Perhaps it is that type of difference that the registry was reflecting upon when it determined to create a code of conduct for the defence. Now, in terms of the conduct of the members of the Office of the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor herself when she appears before Trial Chambers, that conduct is regulated by the statute and the rules, and there are very clear guidelines in there as to what we may or may not do. We may not act purely on political motives because the statute and the rules set up a procedure whereby, before we can indict someone, we must present the evidence and the indictment to a Judge. That Judge must review it and determine that a sufficient level of proof has been presented. When we come to a trial, the Defence, the accused, has the right to raise issues concerning the form of the indictment, has the right to come forward and say, "Based on evidence that has been presented to us, this is a politically motivated indictment which has no evidence to support it," and asks the Trial Chamber to take appropriate action. In regard to other rules perhaps, for example, disclosure, there are very comprehensive disclosure rules that we are obligated to follow. That also sets our standards for behaviour before Trial Chambers. In opposing this Defence request, the Prosecution opposes the request that a Trial Chamber or, indeed, any other organ of this Tribunal, mandate to the Prosecutor that she must prepare some type of code of conduct that then must be subjected to scrutiny by others within this Tribunal. We believe that is an infringement upon the specific independence that was given to her by the statute. That is not to say she does not supervise and oversee those who work for her. That is a matter for her to decide how she is going to carry that out. It is not for the Defence to ask a Trial Chamber to mandate to her how she will do that. Now, in regard to some portion of the Defence counsel's argument here, we certainly would agree that a Trial Chamber may set forward its own rules of behaviour for anyone who comes before the Trial Chamber, both Prosecution and Defence. We are not opposing such a creation of rules. Many courts, many Chambers, have rules that apply to cases coming before those Chambers. That is different than saying this Chamber should order the Prosecutor to come up with something to regulate her own people, contrary to the independence she is given by the statute. Certainly nothing that exists in the current statute or rules precludes an accused from coming forward or a Defence counsel from coming forward and making good faith allegations of misconduct in a particular case before a Trial Chamber. That can be done. There is nothing to preclude that. And this code of professional conduct they speak of does not take the place of that. They already have an effective means to raise any issues they have concerning misconduct on our part. We suggest that this motion is not based on any issues before this Trial Chamber, that it calls for relief that invades the independent functioning of the Office of the Prosecutor, and that it should be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to add anything, Mr. D'Amato?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, we are against you. We are satisfied that the conduct and independence of the Prosecutor is set out under the statute, and it is in the statute that the safeguard for that conduct is to be found. Defence counsel, as has been pointed out, on the other hand, are independent contractors who come for a particular case, and it was no doubt for that reason that it was felt right that there should be a code of conduct in their case. The level playing field, we are satisfied, is provided by statute and code and there is no real distinction between the two. We turn next to evidential matters and two motions from the Prosecutor, the first described as a request in relation to judicial notice, and perhaps it might be convenient if that was introduced by the Prosecution? We have it before us. It relates to mainly documents, as far as I can see. But perhaps, Ms. Hollis, you could deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basically, Your Honour, the Prosecution is asking that this Trial Chamber take judicial notice of, first of all, the fact that the prohibition of the crime against genocide is a pre-emptory norm, and it is my understanding that the Defence does stipulate to that. Secondly, that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ratified the Genocide Convention on 29 August, 1950. It is my understanding the Defence also stipulates to that. As to the other request for judicial notice, basically, Your Honour, they concern the dates upon which certain declarations or actions were taken. In the Defence response to the remaining request for judicial notice, that be would be 3 through 7, the Prosecution is somewhat confused by some of the responses. For example, in their response to number 3, the response is that Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded -- was involved in an illegal succession. We think that perhaps that goes to the import of what they did and not whether or not they took that action on the 6th of March as we are asking for judicial notice of. So, again, we are asking judicial notice that on the 6th of March, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded to the Geneva Convention regarding the prohibition against genocide. The Defence appears to be focusing their response on whether that action was lawful or unlawful, that is, the import of that action. So in that regard, we would suggest it is somewhat non-responsive to our request for judicial notice of the date the action was taken. Concerning number 4, the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence on the 3rd of March of 1992, again we are somewhat confused by the Defence response. It alleges that this was an illegal act. Again, it appears to go to the import of the act rather than whether indeed that declaration was made on that date, which is what we are asking judicial notice of. As to number 5, in that we are asking judicial notice that the European Community recognised the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 6th April, 1992, and that the United States tendered such recognition on the 7th of April, 1992. The Defence, in their response to this, indicates that the European Community and the United States may have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina at those times but that, by that recognition, they somehow caused the conflict. So, again, they seem to be making an argument based upon the import of the recognition rather than disputing the dates that we are asking be judicially noticed and the act that occurred on those dates. As to numbers 6 and 7, the Defence indicates they have been provided no evidence that would verify these requested dates, and we will provide the Defence with that information and perhaps, once they receive it, they can determine whether or not they would stipulate to that judicial notice. So we undertake to provide them with that information so they may make that decision regarding 6 and 7. Again, Your Honour, we would suggest that what we are asking here be judicially noted would be a saving of judicial time and resources, and that we are asking the Court to recognise that on particular dates, certain declarations or recognitions were made. The import of those would have to be developed at trial, and certainly judicial notice of the dates that these declarations or recognitions were made would in no way prevent the Defence, if they choose to make it their defence to argue that other countries caused what happened in the former Yugoslavia, judicial notice of what we are requesting would not preclude them from raising such a defence. So we would ask that as to 3 through 5, that at this time you would take judicial notice of those facts; and as to 6 and 7, we will provide information to the Defence, and then, if necessary, we may come back to you and either have further argument on it or indicate stipulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the items 3 to 7, this is not only the dates that Defence is objecting to, because if you would consider that the only relevant dates are going to be admitted, why is the Prosecutor suggesting it? They're suggesting it to avoid admitting these dates through their expert witnesses. If the expert witness were to testify on these purely political acts, we would get the opportunity to cross-examine them and bring out all of these side issues that are being left to us and you to hear it. But how are we going to get to them? That's the depth of our objection. Would we have them to put witnesses to question the substance or propriety or legality? That's the response. But in their request for judicial notice, there were not dates, there were not how these events came about. Why did they come about? What type of evidence is going to be even necessary for us to consider whether or not April 6th was the date when the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina or United States recognised -- or 7th. I think these are the very important issues. The issue is here: Who precipitated Bosnian civil war and who had enough knowledge and should have had enough knowledge when to act or not to act? Was it government of the United States and Western European nations that jumped to conclusions when they should have known better? Even they were warned by some foremost world diplomats. Or is it Dr. Kovacevic that made the plan? That's what issue is here. They're trying to kind of bypass it. We want a trial on the issues. Please don't take it away from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, may I ask you a question? One point you are contesting is that Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded to the Genocide Convention of 1949 as from the 6th of March, 1992. Would you say that the succession of a State to another State with regard to an International Convention is a legal fact and that this legal fact is well known because the depository of the Genocide Convention, namely the United Nations, has made known to everybody when this succession took place? We all know that the Secretary-General, being the repository on behalf of the UN of all the treaties which have been negotiated and concluded under the auspices of the UN, has the right and duty to give anybody, even private individuals, a document stating when a particular State has succeeded to another State with regard to a particular treaty. So this is a legal fact. Succession of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the Genocide Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your question goes beyond the request that was presented in the request of judicial notice, as I understand it. But I welcome it, and may I just have a short conference with my respected colleague, Professor D'Amato, because he is the authority on the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, before doing so, just please read again number 3 of the Prosecutor's request for judicial notice where it is stated Bosnia and Herzegovina succeeded to the Genocide Convention with an effective date of 6th of March and so on. That is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If you are talking about item 3, Bosnia and Herzegovina committed illegal secession; seceding, split. My idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: It's the wrong word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It is the wrong word. I think, you know, we are talking -- I might have used the wrong word here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are speaking of succession, State succession, succeeded to the Genocide Convention. Not seceded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Seceded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are talking of a different matter, and this is legal fact, as I say. If you look up the relevant UN document, which is an official document, and we are a UN body, a subsidiary body of the Security Council, so we are entitled and actually we are duty-bound to know the legal documents of the UN, you will find this particular date. You will find that it is stated there that Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded to the Genocide Convention, namely, became bound by the Genocide Convention, as from the 6th of March, 1992. It's a legal fact. I don't see why we should not take judicial notice of something that is taught in any university.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason for my objecting is, it's not whether this is a legal fact but an underlying premise is whether or not secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina was illegal under Yugoslav Constitution at that time. If the underlying fact, substance, is illegal, is the form good enough to cover illegal substance? That's what the import of my rejection to accept this proposition. I believe Your Honour is entirely correct, but what I was addressing, I was addressing the substance. If nobody has examined -- and this is, you know, a judicial function, to examine legality of secession, of splintering the country, and subsequent recognition whether or not that was a lawful under international conventions and accords, if that is the substance, if it is saying, "We are going to disregard all of it," only to cloak it with a form, then I would agree with you. But in principle, I cannot, because I don't think that unsavoury practice should be covered with sacrosanct robes of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I point out that, as I say, first of all, there is a misunderstanding here, we are speaking of succession, State succession. In any case, since you have agreed to point 1, namely, that genocide, the crime of genocide, is laid down in a pre-emptory norm of customary international law, not only a rule of customary international law but pre-emptory rule of customary -- which is very strong, and I'm delighted that you accept this proposition, I, in a way, it does not matter -- it matters very little whether or not Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded to the Convention because, in any case, it was bound by the customary rules of international law on genocide. Whether or not it was bound by the Convention, in any case, it was bound by the customary rules. And you did agree that the prohibition of genocide is laid down in a pre-emptory rule. But let us move on to point 4. Would you say that the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence on the 3rd of March, 1992, is an historical fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I've been reading papers in those days but, Your Honour, I don't have independent recollection. And honestly, because we've been so busy preparing for the trial, I didn't get the chance to go through all papers and something to look at it. I know it happened in -- but I can recall an incident that a US congressman came to Chicago and talked to us two days before US recognised the country and says, "President Bush is going to recognise Bosnia. We'd just like to let you know." I know about it. It seems from here that Bosnia declare independence a month before that time. I cannot agree to something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I am sure that you know very well the so-called Keesing's Archives, which is a collection of records of well-known -- they can be found in any library or bookshop and so on. If you look up the Keesing's archives, you will see that it is stated there as a fact, as a fact, as an historical fact, that Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence. I'm not saying that you should accept the legality of this declaration or any legal inference from this fact, but it is a fact. Whether, as I say, they were wrong politically, legally, and so on, is a different issue. And, again, I wonder whether also the recognition by the European Community and by the United States to your mind are not simply facts which may be taken judicial notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The duty of this Tribunal, just as any other court in the world worth its weight, is to examine the facts, and that's what I'm asking of you because trying to say that some political acts are more facts than are facts examined before this court, it's kind of difficult for me to accept. I run away from a political system 25 years ago that kind of had that similar type of an aura of it, and maybe -- I had given up the practice of medicine to become a lawyer; I am devoted to it. That's all I can tell you. Examination of the facts is I think what a trial is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall take judicial notice as follows: One and two are not disputed, so we will take judicial notice of those matters. Three to five, we propose to take judicial notice of these dates. These are matters of fact; they are not matters which are in dispute. The legal import, the legal significance of these dates and these events are, of course, matters entirely to be decided during the trial. But that these things happened on the particular day which it is said they happened, we will take judicial notice of that. As for 6 and 7, in order to expedite matters and not to hold matters up further, we will take judicial notice of those matters but subject to the Prosecution presenting the relevant documents, and we will give the Defence leave to raise the issue again if they wish to do so having seen the documents. But subject to those matters, we will take judicial notice. That brings us to the last motion which may take us beyond the adjournment. I have in mind adjourning in about a quarter of an hour, something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Point of order, Your Honour? There were also some additional matters at the end of my response to their brief where I asked the Court to rule on a few issues, and I don't see that those are on your list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They weren't. But I remember that. We will look at that overnight and see if we can deal with them. That, in fact, Ms. Hollis, brings us to the pre-trial admissions. But before we deal with that and before we leave the matters of judicial notice, it might be helpful to the Trial Chamber if a chronology could be produced. Certainly, experience suggests that a document of that sort is helpful in deciding issues, a chronology of significant events, if the Prosecution would provide such a document? Again, it would have to be produced in the form of a preliminary document, it will be subject to argument and that sort of thing, but it would be useful as a skeleton for us to follow the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that. Do you have a suspense or a deadline for us on that, or just as soon as we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As soon as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pre-trial admission. The motion, together with Attachment "A", being the documents which are referred to, and it seems at a cursory glance there are more than 300 of them, I am merely asking this question: What is the effect of the motion if we were to make the order admitting these documents into evidence? Presumably the effect would be that you would then not have to call any evidence in order to produce them. But deciding the import and effect again will, of course, be a matter entirely for us, the Trial Chamber, but the documents, as it were, would be admitted without further evidence. Am I right in saying that's the effect of what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In large part, that would be, Your Honour. We would certainly not have to bring in witnesses who would testify to the authenticity of the documents. That would already have been accepted by the Trial Chamber. We suspect that with many of the documents, we would have witnesses that would talk about them, so that it would not entirely preclude testimony relating to them but would expedite matters in that they would already have been admitted and, for a substantial number, it is possible we would not then have additional evidence brought forth on them. But in regard to this motion, Your Honour, if I could simply state that the Defence suggestion in their response, that this is a matter that perhaps could be better resolved at a later date after the Defence and the Prosecution have met and discussed the documents one by one, then if a hearing was needed on disputed documents, we could have it; if not, we could simply come forward and say that the Defence and the Prosecution both agree to the introduction of these into evidence. So perhaps this is a matter that would be better dealt with at a later time and dealt with more efficiently after we've had an opportunity to discuss this with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems, if I may say so, a very sensible course. When would it be intended that you would be discussing these matters with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would depend in part on the scheduling of the trial. It would certainly be sometime in the not-too-distant future that we would sit down and discuss these documents with them. One of the points that they made, without taking their argument away from them, but one of the points they made in their response was that they don't believe they're yet in receipt of all the documents. We did provide all of these to them either on the 28th of February or, more recently, on the 20th of April. Now, whether they've actually had a chance to receive them and digest them is a separate matter. I'm sorry, the 28th of January and the 20th of April. So that they have received them, but they perhaps have not been able to fully digest them yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what you would suggest is that we make no ruling on the motion at this time subject to a conference between the parties to resolve the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, and we again are making that in support of the Defence request. I believe that is what they have requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I think we would be minded to do. Does anybody want to say anything about that from the Defence's point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I welcome the suggestion from the Senior Trial Attorney Hollis, and I am the responsible person for this answer. I have been in receipt of the material, I have read all the material that was given to us in January and February, what has been turned over to the Defence before this Trial Chamber was empanelled. But when I looked at this list, I could not just recall half of these documents. I have read just about half of the witness statements that had been given to us about three weeks ago, and that's why I said, you know, I just didn't see them. I'm not saying that they were not sent, I'm not saying that -- maybe my memory is failing, but, you know, I have read them quite a few times. That's why I suggested that a conference indeed would be very proper. What I -- on the substantive -- and I think we can go -- but on the substantive approach of attempting all of this evidence without giving Defence an opportunity to cross-examine not only the foundation but the substance, who authored what, we might be faced in the position the Trial Chamber will have to read a lot of newspaper articles and memos from different committees and whatnot without us ever questioning what is in there and how relevant is this to the indeed very specific charges of complicity and genocide that has been laid out by Professor D'Amato in his response to pre-trial brief. That's why we have to tailor this submission of evidence as to foundation, relevance to the crime that he is charged with. That's why this conference, I welcome it, I expect it to be very productive, but remembering some of the articles, you know, that I read in, you know, they're just too far afield from the charges that are pending against my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That motion will be adjourned for a conference between the parties to be listed at least 28 days before trial, if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, because instead I would welcome it if they could do it within the next few days because I would -- because we had scheduled our time to be here for trial. That material has been given to us, some in January, so it is immense amount of material, that we can get opportunity, because Prosecutor is so much familiar with it, to enable us to digest it now and be prepared later on than to be swamped on the eve of trial, as it could have happened now if we were to proceed today. And I'm not -- you know, I know that they are under the same burden as we are, but as long as we can use this -- allow in the proceedings to deal effectively with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, that is a sensible suggestion, that the matter could be dealt with, if possible, this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we would commend that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That leaves the matter on which we have to rule, which we can do tomorrow morning. It leaves the matter which has to be dealt with in closed session. I don't know whether the Defence are in a position to deal with that, the other motion in relation to matters which have to be dealt with in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: And that other issue for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Keegan or Ms. Hollis, whoever is dealing with this, Mr. D'Amato refers to the matters he raised in answer to the pre-trial brief -- you may remember those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In response to the pre-trial brief, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have, of course, reviewed that and will be able to make initial comments, but we haven't had the time to do any in-depth response to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we could consider it in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we're allowed to simply give our preliminary inputs on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That would be useful. And after that, we'll have a status conference. Bearing in mind that we shall start at 10.00 and we have to finish tomorrow by half past twelve, at least the morning session.
